title: Sudden oxygen desaturation
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Go to the patient first when the saturation alarm sounds and assess breathing, not just the number.
Stay with the patient, support oxygenation as the unit policy allows and clear secretions only when there is a need.
Escalate early if the saturation does not recover, then reassess and document the response.

sources.use: Open RN Nursing Fundamentals 8.3: focused assessment, signs of hypoxia, stay with the client, respiratory monitoring, reassessment
AARC oxygen CPG: oxygen use, monitoring
NEWS2: early warning and escalation of deterioration

Open RN Advanced Skills chapter 6: pleural deterioration and chest drain nursing surveillance paragraphs inspected 2026-11-23. Only differential awareness; no chest tube procedures or decompression algorithm.
FDA public indexed device accuracy limitations; no procedure or numeric threshold inferred.

required_sources: A national guideline or professional standard on responding to acute desaturation in an adult in a critical-care unit
Unit airway-emergency, oxygen and suctioning protocols
Unit's pneumothorax, chest-drain malfunction, and tension-physiology emergency escalation protocol for patients on respiratory support.
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
No source read gives a stepwise sequence for sudden desaturation; the steps are assembled from assessment, monitoring and escalation statements and have not been tested against a protocol.
Oxygen flow, targets and device choice are deliberately not written; they come from the order and policy.
Escalation score thresholds are local and are not written.

The pleural emergency differential was strengthened without adding an independently validated tension pneumothorax diagnosis or invasive procedure: specific thoracic emergencies require local ICU/pleural-team protocols and specialist sign-off.

2026-11-24 AI source-scope check: the case has no artificial airway; removed AARC artificial-airway suction citation and skill link, used the registered Open RN oxygenation source for oral secretion assessment, and removed partial credit for leaving the deteriorating patient. Independent assessment of all scenario choices remains required.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
Open RN chapter 6 is cited for patient-assessment concepts only, independently phrased; textbook tables, figures and procedural steps not reproduced.
setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit who is breathing without a ventilator, receiving oxygen as prescribed.

steps.info: The saturation alarm sounds and the reading is much lower than it was ten minutes ago. The patient is awake and looks worried.

options.text: Go to the patient, remain at the bedside and assess airway, breathing effort, chest expansion symmetry, colour, lung sounds and circulation. Compare the oximeter alarm with the patient rather than relying on the probe alone, and call for urgent help if deterioration is significant.
options.feedback: A rapid fall in oxygen saturation requires patient-first assessment, not an assumption of probe failure. Chest asymmetry or circulatory instability may indicate a pleural or other emergency needing immediate team assistance; oxygen readings must be interpreted with the clinical findings. Poor peripheral circulation and skin pigmentation may affect oximetry accuracy. Assess signal reliability in parallel and seek further measurement if the clinical picture is discordant; do not delay care.
options.consequence: You identify increased breathing effort and a wet cough. Secretions are one possibility, but the team must remain alert to other causes of deterioration.

options.text: Reposition the probe and leave to see whether the number improves.
options.feedback: Checking the probe can help establish signal reliability, but leaving a visibly deteriorating patient without assessing breathing is unsafe. Remain with the patient, reassess promptly and summon help.
options.consequence: A minute passes before you see that the patient really is struggling.

options.text: Silence the alarm because the patient is talking and probably fine.
options.feedback: A patient who can talk can still be hypoxic; early signs of hypoxia include anxiety and restlessness, and the alarm is a call to assess.
options.consequence: The saturation keeps falling and the patient becomes more distressed.

steps.info: The patient has a weak, wet cough, and you can hear secretions. The oxygen device is connected and in place. The saturation is still low.
steps.prompt: What is the best next step?

options.text: Activate urgent help according to the unit pathway, continue prescribed or protocol-authorised oxygen and reassessment, and assess whether the patient cannot clear oral secretions. Only a trained nurse should use the appropriate non-invasive oral suction method under local policy when indicated; do not delay emergency assessment or assume secretions are the sole cause.
options.feedback: This fictional patient is breathing without an artificial airway. Open RN Nursing Fundamentals describes oral suction for retained mouth or pharyngeal secretions. The AARC artificial-airway guideline does not establish suction technique for this patient. Escalate ongoing respiratory compromise and reassess the response.
options.consequence: The responding team assesses the patient and the appropriate secretion-clearance measures; breathing effort and oxygenation are reassessed rather than assuming the problem is resolved.

options.text: Suction repeatedly until the saturation reaches its usual level.
options.feedback: Repeating suction without reassessing indication, patient tolerance and the cause of deterioration is unsafe. Suction is not a substitute for urgent clinical assessment.
options.consequence: The patient becomes more distressed and the saturation falls further during suctioning.

options.text: Increase oxygen or change devices solely to normalize the monitor without reassessing the patient or following the emergency pathway.
options.feedback: Emergency oxygen and breathing support must not be withheld when indicated. Use the authorized emergency pathway, assess the cause and reassess the patient; do not chase a displayed saturation alone.
options.consequence: The underlying respiratory deterioration is not assessed despite changing oxygen delivery.

steps.info: The saturation has come up a little but the patient is still breathing hard. The doctor and the outreach nurse have arrived.

options.text: Give an SBAR handover (what you found, what you did and how the saturation responded), keep monitoring, reassess heart rate, breathing rate, saturation, lung sounds and the patient's own rating of breathlessness, and document what was done and whether it worked.
options.feedback: Reassessment after an intervention includes heart rate, breathing rate, oximetry and lung sounds and asking the patient to rate breathlessness; the effect of interventions is documented.
options.consequence: The team has a clear picture, and the record shows the sequence of events.

options.text: Step back and let the team work; write the notes later.
options.feedback: With continued increased breathing effort, stepping away without a structured transfer of responsibility risks missed deterioration. Provide the responding team with the timeline and ensure ongoing assessment.
options.consequence: The team lacks essential observations and the ongoing monitoring responsibility is unclear.

options.text: Reset the alarm limits so the alarm stops sounding while the team treats the patient.
options.feedback: Alarm limits are set according to the order or protocol; widening limits during an event hides further change.
options.consequence: A further fall in saturation does not trigger an alarm.

learning_points: Go to the patient first: assess the airway, breathing effort, colour, lung sounds and heart rate, and use the oximeter reading as one finding among others.

Stay with the patient, support oxygenation within authorised policy and consider oral secretion clearance only when indicated and within trained scope. Artificial-airway suction techniques do not apply to this case.
Escalate early when the saturation does not recover, and reassess the same parameters after every intervention.
Do not silence alarms or change limits and devices without authority; hand over with SBAR and document the response.

A wet cough does not exclude pneumothorax, an obstructed drain, or other causes of deterioration. New asymmetric chest movement, hypotension or severe respiratory compromise requires urgent skilled response; do not delay for device adjustments or chest radiography.
Poor perfusion or pigmentation-related measurement limitations may affect oximetry; evaluate the patient and signal together, and obtain further assessment when findings disagree.
